items.excerpt: Nagoya University researchers combined machine learning with quantum chemistry to hunt for efficient blue OLED materials, training a model on quantum-chemistry data for 1,000 molecules and then screening more than 17,000 candidates. The AI slashed computational cost and surfaced promising emitters that were then validated experimentally, showing generative screening can accelerate materials discovery.

A reinforcement-learning algorithm continuously monitors error-detection patterns from a quantum processor's qubits and automatically fine-tunes thousands of control settings, letting the machine 'learn from its own mistakes' while a calculation is still running. The approach keeps quantum computers more stable without costly recalibration pauses, a step toward practical fault-tolerant machines.

UCLA researchers built DeepTimeGate, a physics-informed machine-learning framework that images through scattering media by pairing a reconstruction network with a second algorithm that enforces the fundamental rules of physics as a real-time reality check. The method enables high-quality imaging with low-cost cameras, with uses in biomedical imaging and autonomous-vehicle sensing.

Researchers introduced QEWC, a quantum machine-learning framework that uses quantum geometry to stop 'catastrophic forgetting'—the tendency of models to lose earlier skills when trained on new tasks. By anchoring learning to the geometry of quantum states, quantum AI systems can retain what they have learned across sequential tasks.

An open AI competition to predict drug metabolism—specifically whether candidate molecules activate the pregnane X receptor, a mechanism affecting roughly half of marketed drugs—ended in a 28-way statistical tie. The result suggests that dataset quality may matter more than model sophistication for AI drug-discovery predictions, reframing how the field invests effort.
